speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We sought views from the public on the draft Bill earlier this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) has evaluated all the feedback received and incorporated them where they are relevant to the draft text of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 46 of the Bill provides for the change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The last such NOR status will be granted for YA 2020 and expire in YA 2024, because it is a five-year scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Individuals who have been accorded the NOR status and continue to meet the conditions will continue to be granted the NOR tax concessions until their status expire.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 12 of the Bill provides for the change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These tax schemes will also be refined to keep them relevant and to ease compliance burden.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 8, 15 and 17 of the Bill provide for these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As mentioned earlier, MOF regularly reviews and refines the income tax regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will now highlight two changes arising from this periodic review of the tax regime which are found in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is by introducing an option for self-employed commission agents to apply a prescribed deemed expense ratio, which is set at 25% of their gross commission income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Those who do not take up this option can continue to claim tax deduction based on the actual amount of expenses incurred in the production of their commission income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This change, found in clause 22 of the Bill, will take effect from YA 2020 for income earned in 2019.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, to align with international trends, and to improve accountability and promote open justice, tax proceedings before the Courts will no longer be heard privately by default.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also discontinue the practice of redacting taxpayers' names in published decisions of such judicial proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 38 of the Bill provides for the change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Similar changes will be tabled for the GST Act (GSTA) in relation to proceedings before the Courts under GSTA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The changes relating to Court proceedings, under the Income Tax Act and GSTA, will take effect on 1 January 2020.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to outline some significant and urgent housekeeping changes that we must make in definitional interpretations with the current Income Tax Act and the amendments of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Explanatory Note of the Bill used the term "handicapped" and the amendment in clause 29(b) subparagraph used "incapacitated by reason of physical or mental infirmity".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The reference is derogatory and as Members would know well, is not reflective of the current narrative and ground realities of the disability community and our social policies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In case the House thinks that I am just concerned with semantics, let me share why this is more than just a euphemistic concern.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, definitions and terminologies we use in our legislature reflect how far we have come as a society and have an impact on how the rest of the society carve out their responses and examine their attitudes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we must not leave definitional updates as an afterthought as we update our laws.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As the Executive Director of the Disabled Persons Association (DPA) shared with me when I checked with her on this particular definition, "for any law to define disability by incapacitation or to locate the inability to interact in the world within the disabled person goes against the UN Convention on the Rights of People with Disabilities (CRPD) which locates the barriers in the environment and not the person".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore became a signatory of CPRD in August 2013.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, the term "incapacitated by reason of mental infirmity" goes against the spirit of the Mental Capacity Act introduced in 2008.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In section 4(3), the Act says that a lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to (a) a person’s age or appearance; or (b) condition of theirs which might lead others to make unjustified assumptions about their capability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, this discovery I made also unveiled the inconsistency and misalignment of the definition of "disability" across the legislature.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, the Women’s Charter defines an "incapacitated person" as a person who is wholly or partially incapacitated or infirm, by reason of physical or mental disability or ill-health or old age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In general, the English-speaking disability rights movement has moved away from the term "handicapped" and reclaiming and attributing positive associations with the term "disabled" or "disabilities".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is seen as "outdated" by the community in Singapore. "Handicap" is still used across a multitude of legislation, including the Health Sciences Authority Act, Health Products Act, the Copyright Act and so on.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am thankful for the numerous tax relief schemes that we have to support our disability and vulnerable communities, but I urge the Ministry to update the awful definition of "incapacitated" from 1947 and all references to "handicap" to reflect the current social norms.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We should take the lead from the Singapore’s Enabling Masterplan which also implements CRPD.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Masterplan’s definition and terminology of "disability" reflects the current and aspirational needs of the community. "Disability" is defined as "those whose prospects of securing, retaining places and advancing in education and training institutions, employment and recreation as equal members of the community are substantially reduced as a result of physical, sensory, intellectual and developmental impairments." I also urge all other Ministries to review and update all current provisions for our disability community, and in making new laws, to take the lead from the Ministry of Social and Family Development which leads and updates the Enabling Masterplan with the community.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The intent of the scheme is to encourage businesses to send their employees to volunteer and provide services in various areas, such as legal, human resources and accounting, or even general voluntary services for IPCs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, both businesses and IPCs face an administratively onerous process in applying for BIPs, thereby resulting in low usage of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To put this number in context, there are more than 500,000 business entities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to consider the three suggestions below gathered from conversations with community-based organisations and companies that are keen to realise the policy and impact intent of BIPS.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, this scheme is only available for the 610 approved IPCs which are held to a higher governance standard out of 2,277 registered charities in 2018.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A random audit could be conducted to deter abuses.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will also allow charities to distribute this $50,000 deduction tax limit across corporate partners in more meaningful ways that would better meet their beneficiary needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With the current application process, there is a tendency to rush into partnerships on a first-come-first-serve basis.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand from the reply to my Parliamentary Question in August that the Government is currently considering using fixed manhour rates for BIPS to increase the administrative ease of claiming tax deduction under the scheme.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is very much a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But I would further suggest that the value of the voluntary method be tied to the actual value of the voluntary service rendered, independent of the corporate volunteer’s salary.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This value could be preset by the Government in the form.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, BIPS should also consider including food donations, particularly nutritional food donations, which I shared in my speech for the Resource Sustainability Bill last month as part of our climate change strategy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Countries like the United States (US) and France have already legislated tax deductions for food donations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Social enterprises are businesses that have a social and/or environmental agenda woven into their primary business.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They help to reduce inequality and create livelihood opportunities for vulnerable communities by generating income through innovative products and services in the marketplace.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare my interest as the founder of Hush TeaBar, a social enterprise that employs Deaf persons and persons who live with mental health conditions to provide a curated silent tea experience to promote mental wellness and social inclusion at workplaces.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The growth of social enterprises in Singapore has generally been organic because we do not yet have a clear national strategy on this, including recognition of these enterprises as separate legal entities in their own right.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we do not know the total number of social enterprises in Singapore, but we do know from a response to my Parliamentary Question in February that 336 of them chose to be members of the Singapore Centre for Social Enterprises (raiSE) as at March 2018.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Out of these, 92 or 27% had an annual revenue of at least or more than $200,000, including Hush.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I remember having a conversation with an impact investor a few years back who shared that she would not think of investing in Singapore social enterprises since there are already grants given by the Singapore Government through the Tote Board and administered by raiSE.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As much as grants are welcome, they encourage innovations differently from investments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Investments into social enterprises could be encouraged with tax rebates for impact investors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This may also help to shift the mindset from conventional donations to investing in social enterprises and eventually building a larger ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The United Kingdom government introduced the Social Investment Tax Relief in 2014 to help social enterprises attract capital in order to drive and grow their business.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to consider such legislative innovations to incentivise market-driven investments into local social enterprises.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must do more to create the right environment for more of these impact businesses to grow from micro-businesses to small and medium enterprises and eventually bringing our Singapore brand of social innovations overseas as part of our global citizenry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, I would like to quote Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat at the Building our Future Singapore Together Dialogue in June 2019.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I quote, "beyond partnering you in specific areas, we will work with you to create a shared future, one where every Singaporean will have a part to play." Mr Speaker, this commitment must surely include every differently-abled and vulnerable Singaporean by recognising them in a respectful, dignified and consistent manner across our laws and policies, as well as creating enabling environments to invite and support every business and every social enterprise to contribute to a nation that cares.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because the Singaporean society that we want to be is not about bringing people into what already exists but about making a new and better space for everyone to thrive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Ms Anthea Ong mentioned, this is a relatively new scheme introduced in Budget 2016 to encourage businesses to support their employees to volunteer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Since then, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth and the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC) have been exploring ways to refine the scheme and to make the administrative processes more convenient and seamless for both businesses and IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this will address the issues that the businesses and IPCs have been raising about administrative burden and confidentiality concerns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will also serve to encourage businesses to tap on the expertise of their employees and their services to better support the needs of IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We hope these enhancements will reduce the administrative burden on both our IPCs and businesses who are part of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Anthea Ong also offered other suggestions for BIPS, including having food donations recognised as part of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will take all these suggestions into consideration as we continue to improve and finetune this scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, besides BIPS, there are other existing schemes that provide more direct support for charities and IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, under the Bicentennial Community Fund, the Government provides up to $400,000 in matching grants for donations made to each IPC this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Voluntary Welfare Organisations (VWOs)-Charities Capability Fund supports charities in areas, such as governance and the adoption of technology to enhance operational efficiency.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Government agencies overseeing this sector will continue to review the various schemes that we have, be it on the tax side or through grants, and find ways to continue to encourage and promote a more giving society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Anthea Ong also suggested having tax relief for investors of social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides grants and tax incentives, she highlighted the role of impact investors and she suggested having tax reliefs for such investors to encourage the growth of social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Ms Anthea Ong highlighted, we are currently helping social enterprises through raiSE, and the Minister for Social and Family Development had elaborated on this when he responded to a question in Parliament last month on the support provided to help social enterprises to grow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will likewise study Ms Anthea Ong's suggestion on this particular area and see how we can do more to encourage the growth of our social enterprise sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have taken legal advice on this, and there is no doubt about that matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nevertheless, I agree with the Member that language can play an important role in promoting inclusion in society and some of the terminologies do need to be updated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will consider this at the next review of the Income Tax Act.
